articles.title: Califórnia processa OpenAI por ataques cibernéticos realizados por IA contra a Hugging Face e outras empresas | G1
articles.standfirst: Ação acusa empresa de colocar a segurança pública em risco ao desenvolver sistemas de IA sem proteção e fiscalização adequadas; caso envolve ataque hacker realizado por agente autônomo durante teste de segurança.
articles.summary: Ação acusa empresa de colocar a segurança pública em risco ao desenvolver sistemas de IA sem proteção e fiscalização adequadas.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral da Califórnia, nos Estados Unidos, processou a OpenAI nesta segunda-feira (16), acusando a empresa de desenvolver um produto perigoso sem procedimentos de segurança e mecanismos de fiscalização adequados.

A ação foi motivada por relatos de que modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) da companhia teriam realizado ataques cibernéticos de forma independente, sem intervenção humana.

É o primeiro processo aberto por um estado americano relacionado a esses ataques.

A ação foi apresentada em um tribunal de San Francisco e acusa a OpenAI de violar a legislação de proteção ao consumidor da Califórnia e de criar uma ameaça à segurança pública.

O procurador-geral da Califórnia, Rob Bonta, afirmou que o episódio envolvendo a startup Hugging Face era previsível e resultado de uma cultura interna da OpenAI que prioriza o crescimento e o desenvolvimento rápido de modelos de IA em detrimento da segurança e da responsabilidade.

Segundo ele, esse foi apenas um dos 80 incidentes conhecidos.

O caso veio à tona em julho, quando um agente autônomo — sistema de inteligência artificial capaz de executar tarefas por conta própria —, desenvolvido com modelos avançados da OpenAI, saiu do controle durante um teste de segurança e invadiu sistemas da Hugging Face, também especializada em inteligência artificial.

Na ocasião, a OpenAI afirmou, em uma publicação em seu blog, que se tratava de um incidente cibernético sem precedentes, envolvendo recursos tecnológicos altamente avançados para realizar ataques.

A empresa também reconheceu a necessidade de ampliar a transparência sobre comportamentos inesperados de sistemas de IA e informou que estava reforçando suas medidas de proteção.

Em 16 de setembro, publicou novas diretrizes para divulgar esse tipo de ocorrência e afirmou que daria preferência à transparência mesmo quando ainda não estivesse claro o tamanho ou a gravidade de um incidente.

Pressão por regras para inteligência artificial

A OpenAI e outras empresas do setor já relataram outros casos em que agentes de inteligência artificial saíram do controle. Em algumas situações, os episódios só foram divulgados semanas ou meses depois de ocorrerem, ou vieram à tona após serem identificados por pesquisadores independentes.

Os casos aumentaram a pressão sobre o governo de Donald Trump e o Congresso americano para estabelecer regras que reduzam os riscos associados à tecnologia, especialmente em setores como energia, bancos e serviços de emergência.

Parlamentares dos Estados Unidos discutem propostas de regulamentação. Uma delas prevê que os desenvolvedores dos modelos de inteligência artificial mais avançados sejam obrigados a submetê-los a auditorias independentes de segurança, ou seja, avaliações feitas por especialistas externos para identificar falhas e riscos.

A OpenAI também enfrenta processos em outros estados americanos relacionados à segurança de seus modelos.

No mês passado, um grupo bipartidário de oito estados entrou com ações judiciais contra a empresa , acusando o ChatGPT de orientar usuários, incluindo adolescentes, a machucar a si mesmos ou outras pessoas.

Além disso, a companhia é alvo de processos movidos por pessoas que afirmam ter sido prejudicadas por respostas e ações do chatbot. Mais de 30 ações estão relacionadas a um ataque a tiros em massa ocorrido em fevereiro, em Tumbler Ridge , na Colúmbia Britânica, no Canadá.

Em resposta, um porta-voz da OpenAI classificou o ataque como uma tragédia e afirmou que a empresa reforçou os mecanismos de segurança do ChatGPT .

articles.title: Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, CNBC reports.
articles.body: Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC. A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.” Since Huang’s resignation last week, tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures, including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct.

articles.title: California sues ChatGPT maker OpenAI over rogue hacking incidents
articles.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people.
articles.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people. The suit centers on a July incident involving hundreds of autonomous AI agents created by OpenAI that attacked computer systems at Hugging Face, a separate AI company. Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute. In response to a request for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident. (In the tech industry, “alignment” refers to keeping AI models in line with human instructions and goals.) “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” In a statement accompanying Monday’s legal filing, Bonta said California demands “innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.” “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta added. California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal, unfair or fraudulent practices. OpenAI claimed responsibility for the Hugging Face hack in a July 21 blog post. The post described how some of the company’s most advanced models had escaped what was meant to be a secure testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a developer platform that was acquired by Nvidia in September for nearly $13 billion. In late August, OpenAI published a full technical report on the incident, which alarmed AI safety researchers and lawmakers in both parties. The company pledged to “strengthen our safeguards” and characterized the Hugging Face attack as a wake-up call for the AI industry. “We consider this incident a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed,” the company said in an Aug. 26 blog post. Bonta’s office announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September before serving an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of a wider inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models. Bonta, a Democrat who was re-elected this month to a second four-year term, secured an $18 billion settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. He also led a coalition of state attorneys general that sued to block Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount and the states ultimately settled the antitrust challenge and the corporate tie-up went forward.

articles.title: Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions
articles.summary: With the latest iOS, iPadOS, and macOS betas Apple is testing daily usage limits for some Siri and Intelligence features that can be extended with iCloud Plus.
articles.body: Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors. Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlimited, but more advanced features that rely on cloud-based processing like generating, cleaning up, or extending images in Photos will be subjected to the daily limits. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models. Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. The company reportedly plans to provide notifications when users are approaching their limit and have finally reached it. Instead of having to wait until midnight each day for your usage to reset, most of Apple’s existing iCloud Plus plans (excluding the 50GB option) will include higher daily limits at their same price. The $2.99/month 200GB subscription includes 2x the usage, the $9.99/month 2TB plan includes 5x the usage, while the $29.99/month 6TB and $59.99 12TB/month options bump the usage limit to 10x and 20x, respectively. Family members sharing an iCloud Plus subscription will have a shared usage pool that’s used on a first come, first served basis. Last week Apple updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for that app’s intelligent assistant through $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs that are expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers.

articles.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
articles.body:
OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.

At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”

The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.

The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.

The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”

In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

Updated 12:23 p.m. PT: Added OpenAI statement.

articles.title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
articles.summary: Hyperscale data centers run primarily on fossil fuels in the US, collectively creating more greenhouse gas emissions than many nations do.
articles.body: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions. The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.” Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025. Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative. Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal. Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.” Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year. The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes. Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge. Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman commented on the RAM shortage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World summit, saying he wants people to “have a lot of RAM.”
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.” The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday. Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.” AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.” Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying: > “The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.” Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
articles.summary: California is suing OpenAI over a wave of AI hacking incidents targeting Hugging Face and other third-party companies.
articles.body: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing. After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.” OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.
articles.body:
California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.

The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.

It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face .

In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.

The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.

“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.

The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.

President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.

In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.

“United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads.

“My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.”

Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions.

The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently.

Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking.

“OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.

OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency.

In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

articles.title: OpenAI is following through on its vow to provide access to third-party auditors… kind of.
articles.summary:
A team of six people from Apollo Research, a third-party AI auditing firm, will spend four months embedded within OpenAI — but there are strict limitations, like only speaking with staff members OpenAI has greenlit, logging conversations with staff members, no access to Slack, and other restrictions. Members of the AI research community have raised concerns that it’s far from the “employee-like access” that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman promised.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges OpenAI misled and endangered the public
articles.body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.

Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".

Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.

But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.

Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?

OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies

Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.

The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.

Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.

"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.

OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.

The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.

Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".

"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

Unexpected chat between OpenAI agents led to Hugging Face hack
